In the national landscape to take you back in history.
For some of you 2016, the public health agency of Canada began tracking opioid related deaths across our country as well as other harms.
And in 2020 they began to see a significant rise in these deaths across our nation.
Within every province, opioid related deaths being the main contributor.
In 2020 Canada's police leaders through the CACP, the Canadian Association,
Chiefs of Police recommended adopting a public health lead diversionary approach to illicit substance use,
recognizing that substance use disorder as a public health issue.
This same year, public prosecution service of Canada, so the PPSC introduced guideline, which was guideline 5.13 with respect to the prosecution of possession of illicit drugs.
That would be contrary to what's called Section 41 of the Control Drug Substances Act.
And what they put into place in this 5.3 was prosecutors were now required to consider alternatives to possession of charges for illicit drugs.
Unless there is serious manifestations of harm that justified them going ahead with the prosecution.

In May of 2022, Health Canada announced that B.C. the CUP Proidence of British Columbia had been granted a three-year exemption to decriminalize possession of certain illegal drugs for personal use in specific locations.
And this exemption was felt to be a possible find-away solution to the growing opioid crisis across our nation.
It took effect January of 2023. In November of 2022, B.C. 5 received oil, a sent-in part of the bill amended what is called the Control Drug and Substances Act.
And with that approach, it looked at substance abuse to be a health or social issue and not to criminalize it.
But what came into power with that bill is, and is now in place in law, so you understand, is under Section 102 of the CDSA, a police officer, shall instead of laying an information.

So instead of charging somebody against an individual led to have committed an offence under Subsection 41, so simple possession, consider whether it be preferable having regard to the principal set out to take no further action.
To warn the individual, or with the consent of the individual to refer the individual to a program or to an agency or other service provider in the community that may assist that individual.
Back in the province of B.C., their exemption trial process was not having the results that they had hoped for.
The COA toxicity deaths had not decreased through 2023, and unattended consequences of open public drug use consumption became concerning for public safety.
In April of 24, 2024, the B.C. Government submitted an amendment to the federal government to prohibit any amount of illicit drugs in public spaces moving forward with the exemption of a few places.
On April 29, the CACP released the statement supporting that decision, and then on November 27 of 2022 for the CACP solidified.
The stance of non-support for decriminalization of any amount of illicit drugs for personal use.

On our provincial landscape in Saskatchewan, we have a provincial body, it's called the Saskatchewan Association Chiefs of Police, and it's collective body of all municipal police leaders, including the RCMP and the Saskatchewan National Service.
The SACP supports the CACP's new position that was released on November 27.

On its website, you can find it, and I'll summarize that the Saskatchewan Association Chiefs of Police fully supports the Canadian Association Chiefs of Police position on the decriminalization of drugs.
And the SACP believes that decriminalization alone is not an adequate solution to the challenges posed by illicit drug use.
